2:
SAY:
- Read the cultural sensitivity statement aloud, in a calm voice.
- 'In this story we will read about the Coorong and the Ngarrindjeri Country it sits on.'
- 'Some of the language reflects the time it was written, not how we speak today.'

DO:
- Pause briefly so students take it in.
- Move on without inviting discussion.

TEACHER NOTES:
Deliver as a one-minute orientation. Not a discussion task.

SENSITIVITY ADVISORY:
- What it is: references to deceased persons, historical perspectives, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures.
- Framing language: see SAY.
- Watch for: students who may have personal or cultural connections; signs of discomfort during reading.
- Protocol: pause if a student is distressed, offer a quiet seat or water, let the student step out and rejoin without comment.

WATCH FOR:
- Body language at the moment of reading.

[Stage: Lesson Orientation]
7:
SAY:
- 'Today we are reading more of Storm Boy, learning two new words, and learning to take notes using keywords, abbreviations and symbols.'
- Read each Success Criterion aloud and point as you go.
- 'If shorthand feels new, that is okay. We will build it together.'

DO:
- Point to each SC.
- Tap the note-taking criterion twice so students hold it as today's writing focus.

TEACHER NOTES:
Note-taking is a transferable skill assessed in the booklet task.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot say the note-taking goal back; flag for extra modelling later.

[Stage: LI and SC]
8:
SAY:
- 'On your desk: pencil, booklet and novel, mini whiteboard and texta.'
- 'Thumbs up when you are ready.'

DO:
- Scan for thumbs.

TEACHER NOTES:
Ready-to-learn check.

[Stage: Materials]
9:
SOURCES:
- Ochre Education Text Level Reading guide.

SAY:
- 'We are about to read more of Storm Boy. Listen and follow along.'

DO:
- Settle the class with novels open.

TEACHER NOTES:
Reading mode is teacher choice.

[Stage: Text-Level Reading]
10:
SAY:
- 'We are reading pages 67 to 69 of Storm Boy now.'
- 'I will pause where I have marked. Listen for words that are new.'

DO:
- Pre-mark your novel with pause points and queries before the lesson.
- Read at a steady pace; pause where marked, ask a planned query, take 2 to 3 responses, keep reading.
- Note any vocabulary students flag.

TEACHER NOTES:
No handbook supplied to this notes pass. Confirm pause points using your Literature Study Guide before teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students losing the page.
- Trouble with multi-clause sentences.

[Stage: Read-Aloud]
11:
SAY:
- 'Two new words from this part of the story. Listen and we will use them.'

DO:
- Display and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Today's words are stench and rotting.

[Stage: Vocabulary]
12:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is stench. Say it with me. Stench.'
- 'A stench is a very bad smell, especially of something decaying. It is a noun.'
- 'In Storm Boy, the stench of their gunpowder hung on the still air like a black fog of rotting smoke.'
- Ask: 'Say stench with me.' Expected: 'Stench.'

DO:
- Pull a face that shows a bad smell to anchor the meaning.
- Run affixes: 'stenches' (plural).
- Point to associations: bad smell, stink, smelly.

TEACHER NOTES:
A stench is much stronger than 'a bad smell'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students saying 'sten-ch' as two syllables; model the single sten-ch sound.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
13:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. The stench of the garbage bin was so strong that we had to take it out right away.'
- Ask: 'Now make the face you would make if you smelled that. Hold it for me.'

DO:
- Scan faces. Look for scrunched noses and tight mouths.
- Cold call one student to describe what their face is showing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who keep a neutral face; remind them stench is a very bad smell.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
14:
SAY:
- 'Think of a time you smelled a bad stench. Picture it.'
- 'When I tap the bell, silently act out your reaction.'

DO:
- Model your own bad-smell reaction first.
- Give 30 seconds of think time.
- Invite three or four volunteers to act.
- Ask: 'What told you that was a bad smell?' Expected: scrunched nose, hand to face, holding breath.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not want to act; let them mime in their seat.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
15:
SAY:
- 'Two scenarios. Which might give you a bad stench?'
- 'A: When food in the fridge has gone out of date.'
- 'B: When you bake a chocolate cake.'
- Ask: 'Show me A or B. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: A.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is A a bad stench?' Expected: 'because old food rots and rotting things smell bad.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick B because they like cake; redirect to the meaning.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
16:
SAY:
- 'Complete the sentence. The stench of the old lunch box blank.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, an example appears.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'caused all of the children to hold their noses.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing pleasant outcomes; redirect to stench.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
17:
SAY:
- 'A stench is one of these. Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: a stale smell. Two: a very bad smell. Three: a pleasant smell. Four: an unusual smell.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why two and not one or four?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me what stench means.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 2.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 2 and review the meaning.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 1 (stale) thinking it is the same as bad.
- Reteach with examples: 'Stale means old or flat - like stale bread. Stench is much stronger.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing 4 (unusual); not all unusual smells are stenches.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
18:
SAY:
- 'Three sentence stems with stench. Complete each in your own words. Three minutes.'
- 'Stem one: The stench filled the room, but...'
- 'Stem two: The stench filled the room, so...'
- 'Stem three: The stench filled the room because...'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Cold call three students - one for each stem.
- Reveal modelled completions.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show + Cold Call
Script:
- 'Hold up your three completions.'
- Scan for: 80% match a very-bad-smell context and the conjunction.
PROCEED:
- Move to rotting.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students fail to match the conjunction (using because for a result).
- Reteach with the rule: 'But shows contrast. So shows result. Because shows reason.'
- Re-check: 'Rewrite one stem.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write 'I smelled bad' for all three; push for unique completions.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
19:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is rotting. Say it with me. Rotting.'
- 'To rot is to make or go bad. Rotting is happening right now - going bad. It is a verb.'
- 'In Storm Boy, the stench of gunpowder hung on the still air like a black fog of rotting smoke.'
- Ask: 'Say rotting with me.' Expected: 'Rotting.'

DO:
- Hold up your fingers in a pinch and slowly close them to mime decay.
- Run affixes: 'rotten, rotted'.
- Point to associations: decay, decompose, mouldy.

TEACHER NOTES:
Rotting (going bad) vs rotating (turning) - clarify only if it surfaces.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
20:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. The rotting leaves in the garden created a strong, unpleasant smell.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, draw a picture of those leaves and add an arrow to where the smell is coming from.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Look for brown, decaying leaves with smell lines.
- Ask one student to describe their drawing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students drawing fresh green leaves; redirect to rotting.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
21:
SAY:
- 'Two sentences. Which is correct?'
- 'Sentence one: The old tree stump in the yard was slowly rotting away.'
- 'Sentence two: She thought the rotting sunshine was delightful.'
- Ask: 'Show me one or two. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 1.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is sentence two wrong?' Expected: 'sunshine cannot rot.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick 2 because of 'delightful'.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
22:
SAY:
- 'When something is rotting, it is going bad.'
- Ask: 'Where may you have seen something rotting? Tell your partner.'
- 'Example on the slide: I saw rotting bananas in the bottom of the fruit bowl.'

DO:
- Time partner talk for 90 seconds.
- Cold call three students.
- Look for: rotting fruit, rotting wood, rotting leaves, rotting food.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with no example; nudge them to think of the kitchen or garden.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
23:
SAY:
- 'Two pictures. Which piece of wood is rotting?'
- Ask: 'Show me A or B. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to defend their choice; look for 'because the wood is brown, soft, falling apart'.

TEACHER NOTES:
The correct answer depends on the images on the slide - choose the wood that looks decayed.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the older-looking wood without checking for decay markers.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
24:
SAY:
- 'Which word fits best with rotting? Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: new. Two: spoiled. Three: used. Four: fresh.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why two?' Expected: 'spoiled food has gone bad.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me which word fits best with rotting.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 2.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 2.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 3 (used) because used items can be old.
- Reteach with the contrast: 'Used means it has been used but might still be good. Spoiled means gone bad.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick 1 (new) or 4 (fresh) - both are opposites.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
25:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 18 Vocabulary.'
- 'Complete the tasks for stench and rotting.'

DO:
- Hand out booklets.
- Set timer.
- Circulate; read first 2 to 3 answers per student.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: pair with a peer to talk through one example for each word before writing.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write one sentence that uses both stench and rotting together.

TEACHER NOTES:
Flag students who cannot use either word; they need extra modelling in the note-taking segment.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying examples from earlier slides.

[Stage: You Do | Vocabulary]
26:
SAY:
- 'Now we move to note taking. The skill today is taking a long sentence and turning it into short, useful notes.'

DO:
- Display and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Note-taking is the writing focus and the booklet task.

[Stage: Sentence-Level Writing]
27:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'Note taking has five moves. Listen for each one.'
- 'Actively listen or read.'
- 'Use single words or short phrases.'
- 'Identify keywords or main points.'
- 'Summarise in your own words.'
- 'Use headings to organise your notes.'

DO:
- Point to each move as you read it.
- Ask: 'Where have you taken notes before?' Take two responses.

TEACHER NOTES:
Note-taking is a skill that improves with practice. Emphasise short and 'in your own words'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think note taking means copying everything.

[Stage: I Do | Note-Taking Purpose]
28:
SAY:
- 'Why do we take notes? Four reasons.'
- 'Planning and preparing for writing.'
- 'Organising thoughts and ideas.'
- 'Staying focused on the task.'
- 'Clarifying and remembering information.'
- Ask: 'Tell your partner: which reason matters most to you right now?'

DO:
- Time partner talk for 60 seconds.
- Cold call three students.
- Capture good answers on the board.

TEACHER NOTES:
Students who see why a skill matters use it better.

[Stage: We Do | Purpose]
29:
SAY:
- 'Look at this note: Mr P plus S Boy equals best friends.'
- Ask: 'Is this quality note taking? Thumbs up or down. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: thumbs up.

DO:
- Scan thumbs.
- Ask: 'Why is this good?' Expected: uses plus for and, equals for is, abbreviates Storm Boy and Mr Percival.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Thumbs Up or Down
Script:
- 'Quality notes? Thumbs up or down.'
- Scan for: clear majority thumbs up.
PROCEED:
- Confirm and explain why it works.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students think notes need full sentences.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Notes are short. Symbols and abbreviations save time.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think shorter is always better; balance with 'must still make sense to you.'

[Stage: CFU | Note Quality]
30:
SAY:
- 'Look at this note: Mr Percival flew happily overhead.'
- Ask: 'Is this quality note taking? Thumbs up or down. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: thumbs down.

DO:
- Scan thumbs.
- Ask: 'Why is this not good?' Expected: 'no abbreviations, no symbols, has filler words like happily.'
- Compare with the previous example.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think this is fine because it is grammatically correct; stress notes use shorthand.

[Stage: CFU | Note Quality]
31:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'Keywords and phrases tell us the main idea of a sentence.'
- 'Often they answer: who, what doing, when, where, why and how.'
- 'I am going to find the keywords in a sentence soon.'

DO:
- Point to the question words.
- Use the colour coding chart from earlier in the deck if it is on display.

TEACHER NOTES:
Foundation skill before students can take notes.

[Stage: I Do | Keywords]
32:
SAY:
- 'Which option correctly describes keywords? Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: tell you descriptive details.'
- 'Two: include conjunctions and connector words.'
- 'Three: tell you the main idea.'
- 'Four: add detail to the sentence.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 3.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why three?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me what keywords do.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 3.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 3.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 1 or 4 because keywords sound descriptive.
- Reteach with the metaphor: 'Descriptive details add flavour. Keywords are the bones of the sentence.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick 2 (conjunctions); these are the connectors we erase.

[Stage: CFU | Keywords]
33:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. The sentence is: As the captain slowly said his goodbyes, he made sure he scratched Mr Percival's neck.'
- 'Step one: read the sentence.'
- 'Step two: erase the connector words.'
- 'Step three: identify the keywords using who, what doing, when, where, why and how.'

DO:
- Read the sentence aloud.
- Frame the three steps as the routine students will follow.

TEACHER NOTES:
The next two slides reveal the steps live.

[Stage: I Do | Keywords Routine]
34:
SAY:
- 'Step two. Watch me erase the connector words.'
- 'As the - gone. Slowly - that is descriptive, gone. He made sure he - that is repeating the subject, gone.'
- 'What I keep: captain said his goodbyes, scratched Mr Percival's neck.'

DO:
- Cross out connector words on the board version.
- Show the trimmed sentence next to the original.

TEACHER NOTES:
Connectors include: as, the, and, but, so, while.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who erase content words; remind them connector words join, while keywords carry meaning.

[Stage: I Do | Erase Connectors]
35:
SAY:
- 'Step three. Identify the keywords - who, what doing, where.'
- 'Who: captain, Mr Percival.'
- 'What doing: said goodbye, scratched neck.'
- 'My note: Captain said goodbye, scratched Mr P neck.'

DO:
- Highlight each keyword as you say it.
- Show the final note in shorthand on the board.

TEACHER NOTES:
Students should see the full sentence become a note.

[Stage: I Do | Identify Keywords]
36:
SAY:
- 'Now we do one together. Sentence: The storms returned to the cold south, the sun warmed the sandhills, and spring returned to the countryside.'
- 'Step one: read the sentence with me.'
- 'Step two: erase the connector words. Take the lead from your partner.'
- 'Whiteboards. Two minutes.'

DO:
- Read the sentence chorally.
- Time partner work.
- Take 1 to 2 attempts on the board.

[Stage: We Do | Erase Connectors]
37:
SAY:
- 'Step two reveal. We erase: the, to, and, returned to (one of the times).'
- 'What we keep: storms returned cold south, sun warmed sandhills, spring returned countryside.'
- 'Whiteboards: write the trimmed sentence. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Reveal on screen.
- Scan boards. Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who keep too many connectors; nudge them to be ruthless.

[Stage: We Do | Trimmed]
38:
SAY:
- 'Step three. Identify the keywords using who, what doing, when, where, why and how.'
- 'Whiteboards: write your shorthand note. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal a sample note: 'storms - cold south, sun - sandhills, spring - countryside.'
- Cold call one student to share theirs.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write a full sentence again.

[Stage: We Do | Note]
39:
SAY:
- 'Two options of keywords. Which is correct?'
- 'Sentence: But when Storm Boy heard the captain's plan, he wouldn't go.'
- 'Option one highlights one set of words. Option two highlights another.'
- Ask: 'Show me one or two. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why did you choose that one?'
- Confirm the option that captures who (Storm Boy), what doing (heard plan, would not go), and drops connectors (but, when, the, he).

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1 or 2
Script:
- 'Which option shows the correct keywords?'
- Scan for: clear majority on the option that drops connectors and keeps content words.
PROCEED:
- Confirm and review who/what doing.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students keep the connectors because they think they help meaning.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Connectors join ideas in a full sentence, but in notes they take up space without meaning.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

TEACHER NOTES:
The correct option depends on slide rendering - confirm before teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the option that includes 'but' or 'when'.

[Stage: CFU | Keywords]
40:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'Abbreviations are shortened versions of words. We use them to save time.'
- 'Some you may know: AM and PM, Jan, Feb, Dec, NSW, Vic, WA, Rd, St, cm, km, tsp, kg.'
- Ask: 'Which one do you already use?'

DO:
- Read each abbreviation pair.
- Take two responses.

TEACHER NOTES:
Abbreviations are everyday tools, not just for school.

[Stage: I Do | Abbreviations]
41:
SAY:
- 'Brainstorm appropriate abbreviations for Storm Boy. Whiteboards.'
- 'Three options: Storm B, S Boy, SB.'
- Ask: 'Which would you use? Why? Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Cold call three students for their pick and reason.
- Discuss: SB might be confused with someone else. Storm B and S Boy are clearer.

TEACHER NOTES:
An abbreviation must still be readable to you when you come back later.

[Stage: We Do | Abbreviations]
42:
SAY:
- 'Brainstorm abbreviations for Mr Percival. Three options: Mr Percy, MP, Mr P.'
- Ask: 'Pick one and write why on your whiteboard. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Cold call three students.
- Discuss: MP might mean Member of Parliament. Mr P keeps the title and is short.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the shortest without thinking about clarity.

[Stage: We Do | Abbreviations]
43:
SAY:
- 'Four abbreviations. Which word do they highlight?'
- 'H over Way, Hd slash Away, H dash A, Hide-Away.'
- Ask: 'Whiteboards. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Hide-Away.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Which abbreviation would you actually use? Why?'
- Discuss the trade-off between short and clear.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not link abbreviations to the original.

[Stage: We Do | Abbreviations]
44:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'Revising shorthand techniques. Read each one with me.'
- 'Forward slash means new idea. Plus or ampersand means and. Equals means is, equal, or same. Right arrow means leads to or causes. Up arrow means increase. Down arrow means decrease. B slash c means because. W slash o means without. W slash means with.'

DO:
- Choral read each symbol pair.
- Anchor on a wall display so students can refer back.

TEACHER NOTES:
Keep the chart visible for the rest of the lesson.

[Stage: I Do | Shorthand]
45:
SAY:
- 'Four notes on the slide. Do they correctly use the symbols? Talk to your partner.'
- 'Mr P plus S Boy walked 2 beach.'
- 'Mr P equals S Boy played happily.'
- 'Sun down arrow / moon up arrow.'
- 'Mr P staying right arrow S Boy happy.'
- Ask: 'Whiteboards: thumbs up or thumbs down for each. Then the reason.'

DO:
- Time partner talk for 90 seconds.
- Discuss each: 1 yes, 2 no (equals does not mean played), 3 yes, 4 yes.
- Cold call students to defend their thumbs.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Thumbs Up or Down + Cold Call
Script:
- 'For each note, thumbs up if it works, thumbs down if not.'
- Scan for: students recognising the equals issue in note 2.
PROCEED:
- Move to using shorthand to write notes.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students think any symbol can replace any word.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Equals means is or same. Played is an action - we cannot use equals.'
- Re-check: 'Thumbs up or down for note 2.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who give up on the activity; pair them with a partner.

[Stage: CFU | Symbols]
46:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. Sentence: Everyone was happy for the rest of the year.'
- 'I find the keywords: every1, happy, rest of year.'
- 'I add my symbols: every1 happy = rest of year.'
- 'I check it makes sense when I read it back.'

DO:
- Click to reveal the note.
- Read both versions aloud.

TEACHER NOTES:
The next four slides are We Do for shorthand.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot read the note back; that means it has lost meaning.

[Stage: I Do | Note Build]
47:
SAY:
- 'We do one together. Sentence: Mr Percival would fly around their hiding place to help the ducks, warn them in time, and keep them away from the shooters.'
- 'On your whiteboards, take a note using keywords, abbreviations and symbols. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Reveal: 'Mr P fly around hiding pl 2 help ducks + warn in time leads-to keep away from shooters.'
- Cold call one student to read theirs.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who keep all words.

[Stage: We Do | Note Build]
48:
SAY:
- 'Sentence: The shooters were all over the Coorong.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Reveal: 'Shooters = all over Coorong.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write 'shooters were all over' - 'were' becomes the equals sign.

[Stage: We Do | Note Build]
49:
SAY:
- 'Sentence: Mr Percival hated the shooters, and he bothered them whenever he could.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Reveal: 'Mr P hated shooters leads-to bothered when could.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using plus where the meaning is cause-and-effect.

[Stage: We Do | Note Build]
50:
SAY:
- 'Sentence: Without Mr Percival's help, the ducks would not be safe.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Reveal: 'Ducks = not safe w/out Mr P.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who spell out 'without'; remind them w slash o saves time.

[Stage: We Do | Note Build]
51:
SAY:
- 'Two options of notes for this passage.'
- 'Passage: Sometimes he stared at them rudely until they lost patience and chased him away.'
- 'Option 1: Sometimes Mr P stared rudely = until lost patience up-arrow chased away.'
- 'Option 2: Mr P stared rudely leads-to lost patience + chased away.'
- Ask: 'Show me one or two. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is option 1 wrong?' Expected: 'equals does not match the meaning.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1 or 2
Script:
- 'Which option uses shorthand correctly?'
- Scan for: clear majority on 2.
PROCEED:
- Move to the booklet task.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 1 because it has more symbols.
- Reteach with the rule: 'More symbols is not better. Each symbol must match the meaning.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the option that looks fancier without checking meaning.

[Stage: CFU | Note Quality]
52:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 18 Sentence Level Writing.'
- 'Complete the note-taking tasks. Use keywords, abbreviations and symbols every time.'
- 'Read each sentence first, then trim, then add symbols, then check it makes sense.'

DO:
- Set timer.
- Circulate; read first 2 to 3 notes per student.
- Pull a small group if students are still keeping full sentences.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: provide a partially trimmed version of each sentence; students just add symbols and abbreviations.
- Extra Notes: pair with a peer.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: take a paragraph from today's reading and turn it into a list of three notes.

TEACHER NOTES:
The booklet is the You Do for note-taking.

WATCH FOR:
- Notes that cannot be read back later.
- Students inventing symbols; allow if they can explain.

[Stage: You Do | Booklet]
